title: Homework routine for learning disabilities | ELUM
description: When your child hesitates over homework, make starting easier before cutting the amount. A homework routine for learning disabilities and slow learners.
keywords: homework routine, learning disability homework, slow learner homework, homework habits, homework checklist for kids, how to start homework
heading: Homework routine: start one step at a time
lede: Your child may not dislike homework. They may just be stuck, not knowing where to begin.

sections.heading: "Do your homework" is too big
paragraphs: Homework hides steps you can't see, like opening the bag, finding the planner, reading what to do and taking out the right book. If these steps are hard, studying never even starts.
Bring the hidden steps out onto cards, and your child only has to do one at a time.

sections.heading: How to make a homework routine
list: Set the place first. Same desk, same time, every day
Make the first card very easy. Just "sit at your desk" counts as starting
Make the amount visible. "One page of math" instead of "do math"
Add a break card. After each subject, drink water or stretch
End with packing the bag. Tomorrow morning gets easier

sections.heading: When reading is hard
paragraphs: If reading is a struggle, the card pictures and the read-aloud voice can help. ELUM reads each card's sentence aloud, and you can also record it in your own voice.

sections.heading: See what's done
paragraphs: As checked cards add up, your child can see "I did this much." Even on days when not everything gets done, praise what was done. Tomorrow, start from the next card.

cards.title: Action card example: doing homework

items.title: Pack your bag
items.body: Put your homework in your bag

cards.reward: All done: 15 minutes of favorite play

faq.q: Homework is different every day. What then?
faq.a: Keep the frame the same, like 'sit → check → do it → pack the bag,' and change only the middle cards to fit that day.
Try making each card smaller. If 'one page' is too long, change it to 'three problems.' A size your child can finish comes first.
